# Your First Pipeline

Build a small end-to-end exploratory pipeline over incident records: generate a
sample, ingest it, clean the obvious problems, summarize it (incidents per kind,
severity distribution), and plot the result. Along the way, meet the two tools
this course leans on for exploratory work: Polars for dataframes and
Vega-Altair for charts.

-   A pipeline is ingest → clean → explore → summarize → communicate.
-   Each stage is a small, checkable step; the next stage trusts the last.
-   The ecology twin has the same shape: observations per species instead of
    incidents per kind.

## Make a sample

-   A fixed seed makes the pseudo-random sequence reproducible, so this lesson
    runs the same every time and the numbers below can be checked against the
    output.
-   Generate the sample inline so the lesson is self-contained; a real pipeline
    would read this from a file or an API instead.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=make_sample >}}

-   The coordinate ranges pin the incidents to south-eastern Australia, the same
    region the full generator uses; that is an assumption written down rather
    than hidden in the code.

## Ingest

-   Ingest brings raw records into a dataframe. Here we round-trip through CSV
    so `read_csv` is the ingest step; an API or a database would substitute for
    the file.
-   `head` shows the first rows; the schema it prints is the contract the rest
    of the pipeline relies on.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=ingest >}}

## Clean

-   Cleaning is its own lesson; this synthetic data has little to fix, so
    profile first: check the types and count missing values.
-   The one real clean-up is parsing `timestamp` from a string into a datetime,
    so ordering and date arithmetic work later.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=clean_profile >}}

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=clean_parse >}}

## Explore

-   `select` picks columns; `filter` picks rows. Both return a new frame and
    leave the original untouched.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=explore_select >}}

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=explore_filter >}}

-   `high.shape` is the number of rows and columns: the filter keeps only the
    most severe incidents.

## Summarize

-   `group_by` plus an aggregation collapses many rows into one row per group.
-   Count per kind is the headline number: which incident type is most common?

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=summarize_kind >}}

-   The severity distribution is the same operation on a different column.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=summarize_severity >}}

## Reshape

-   `pivot` spreads one column's values across the columns, turning a long table
    into a wide one. Here the severity counts become a matrix with one row per
    kind.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=reshape >}}

-   A `null` cell means no incident of that kind had that severity; the row and
    column totals are the summaries computed above.

## Communicate

-   Altair turns a summarized frame into a chart with one declaration: encode
    the x and y channels and the notebook renders it.
-   `kind` is nominal (`N`) so each value is a separate bar; `len` is
    quantitative (`Q`) so bar height is a measured value. `sort="-y"` orders the
    bars tallest first.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=plot >}}

## Check the answer

-   Every pipeline ends by checking its answer against something known. The
    synthetic data gives us ground truth: the counts must sum to the number of
    rows, and every kind must appear.

{{< inc pipeline/pipeline.py mark=check >}}

-   The ecology twin runs the same stages with `observations` grouped by
    `species`, so "count per kind" becomes "count per species" and the chart
    labels species on the x axis; only the column names change.
